utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution. I appear with Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo. Mr. Niemann will be joining us later this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Could we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey. I am here on behalf of Esad Landzo, along with my esteemed counsel, Ms. Nancy Boler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly invite the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, you may proceed. ARIF SULTANIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 163. (Handed). This is the document that you were shown yesterday by Defence counsel in direct examination and I just have a couple of questions about it. First, did you actually see this document in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was this order carried out? In other words, is it the case that all communication units were taken from the existing communication centres and moved into the Zlatar facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day, but within a short period of time -- actually, at the end of July -- no, end of June, as the HVO separated from the TO, they split, and they moved the communications centre. I am not quite sure whether this was within five days, but I do know that they moved their own communications centre, because of the frequent shelling and the lack of safety -- if we had only one communication centre -- so we needed several. So, when the HVO split from the TO and formed its separate command, then this communications centre was set up on Mount Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, the question is whether this order was carried out. Did you carry out the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I was not the person carrying out the order, because this order was to be carried out by Mr. Vlado Azinovic, who was chief of communications in HVO, and Mr. Muhamed Alic was supposed to ensure telephone lines -- the lines connecting that facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I understand you, it was never the case that all communication units were moved to Zlatar, although it is the case that some weeks later the HVO moved some of their communication equipment to Zlatar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already said, in the town of Konjic, there were several communication centres, such as the MUP, the operational centre, the centre for warning and information, and the centre of the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask you more directly. It is the case that the TO communication centres were not moved to Zlatar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, when this communications centre was transferred, because a day or two after this a decision was taken not to form the communications centre at Zlatar because the HVO forces later I think -- and this is clear to you -- they moved later on, they separated from the TO and that is how they formed this communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am correct that what happened is that this order was issued and it was never carried out and a couple of days later there was a decision made to move the TO communication facilities to Mr. Delalic's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you were following what I said earlier on, then it is clear that the TO communications centre was later moved to Mr. Delalic's house -- parallel with the time when this communications centre was being formed at Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When the communications centre was moved to Mr. Delalic's house, was there a written order, like this one -- like the one about Zlatar? Did you see a written order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it, because, as I said, the head of communications was somebody else -- not me. Therefore, whatever I was told by the person in charge of communications, I implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you saw this order of 8 June, but you never saw the subsequent order; correct? You just did as you were told; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly yesterday that the person who told you that all the equipment was to be moved to Mr. Delalic's house was Mustafa Bajgoric -- I may be pronouncing that name incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person, Mustafa Bajgoric, did not tell me that this equipment had to be moved to Mr. Zejnil Delalic's house, because that person at the time was in Mostar. Since we as a company had two Harrison-type installations, one of these was used by the HVO and the other was supposed to be transferred to Konjic and this is what I discussed with Mr. Mustafa Bajgoric. I apologise, but please allow me to continue. We discussed where we should move it -- I beg your pardon -- so, with the head of communications and with the TO bodies, we were discussing which would be the best position and, since these other centres had been distributed in town, and in view of the installations that Mr. Delalic already had in his house -- electrical installations -- he had a generator -- since he needed this generator earlier on, he had used it for his discotheque, so I proposed that this communications centre be moved there, as it was the safest place -- even though there was some shelling around there, but not any direct hits at the house. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, who exactly from the TO ordered you to move this equipment to Mr. Delalic's house, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Azinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, after the communications equipment was moved to Mr. Delalic's house, in addition to the powerful radio equipment that you have already talked about, am I correct that the communications centre could receive and send faxes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you are not right, because the communications centre could not send faxes. Fax messages used telephone lines and Konjic did not have telephone connections with Sarajevo or Mostar, and I already said that, when I arrived at Mr. Delalic's house, I did not see any fax machine. I did see a radio station and equipment that had arrived with the convoy from Zagreb and these radio transmitters needed to be distributed among the units and energy supply ensured for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We did listen to your direct testimony. Sometimes, when I am asking you a question, I do not need you to give details about other things that I have not asked you about. If you think it is necessary to give a fair answer, you can give them, but it is prolonging the process. Do I understood you; during the entire time you worked at the communications centre, the communications centre could neither receive nor send faxes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I want to make sure this is for the entire time period, because I think this is an important point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said earlier on that I was not there all the time. Occasionally, when I needed to assemble something or to repair any of the installations or set them in operation, I said that the fax was not working there. Secondly, if I am speaking under oath, I think that if I was just to say "Yes" or "No", I would not be conveying the substance of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, do I understand you that you do not know for sure whether or not the communications centre could receive or send faxes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure that that communications centre could not receive or send faxes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the communications centre receive or send telegrams or telexes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could send telegrams by means of short-wave radio -- it could do that by means of radio waves, but it could not send telexes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when written orders were delivered by messengers to Konjic, did those written orders also come to the communications centre; in other words, was it a sort of clearing house for written orders also that came through messengers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure that the question is clear. Do you mean all the couriers who brought messages, they first came to the communications centre? Ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When couriers came from other places outside Konjic to deliver messages, would they go to the communications centre, or would they deliver the message right to whomever it was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Messages that arrived and had to do with the communications centres and that had to be forwarded from there were brought to the communications centre, but I was not there all the time. I had a broad field of activity, so I was not there and I cannot know whether all those messages came there, but if there were messages that had to be sent on by radio waves, then they would come to the communications centres and would be forwarded by radio, but I believe that messages that applied to anyone in town would be handed directly to the addressee -- that is my assumption -- I am not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know, Sir, if Sarajevo was sending an order to the TO commander -- would it go through your communications centre or not, or do you just not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure of that -- I do not know. That was not my speciality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the TO have ways to communicate with Sarajevo other than through the radio at the communications centre; in other words, did the TO have its own separate equipment such that it could communicate directly with Sarajevo without going through the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the communications centre of the TO, so I do not see why you are mentioning any other TO. This was the TO communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that, whenever the TO wanted to communicate with Sarajevo, they would do it through the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you said yourself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, were the officers of a company named INDA-BAU ever used to facilitate communications that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, I did not understand it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not any officers of a company called INDA-BAU located in Zagreb, do you know whether or not those officers and their communications equipment were ever used to facilitate communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please explain what INDA-BAU is -- what is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you do not know, all you have to do is say, "I do not know".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I have heard of this word, of this company and of that communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. Am I correct that the communications centre was used not just by the TO but also on occasion by the war presidency and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the event that their power was down, or due to shelling, one of the centres was incapacitated, then they would also use this centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that the communications centre also served as a kind of office and, indeed, was considered by some persons, including persons who worked there, as the headquarters for the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not considered as an office, nor was it an office, but, when a message needed to be sent on, a courier would bring it and it would be forwarded by radio, because please bear in mind that there was also here a workshop -- my own workshop for the repair of installations, and also the people manning the installations slept there, so it could not be an office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me, though, that typists worked there, for instance, and they would type orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you consider the personnel using the communications equipment as typists, then, yes, they did send orders by radio waves, but they cannot type them if they did not have typewriters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, where were the headquarters of the TO -- where were they located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO command would move around -- while the TO and HVO were together, they were near the bus station, but after the split, the TO was relocated just away from that building -- a short way away from the building, to a local school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that meetings were sometimes conducted in the communications centre, both downstairs and upstairs of Mr. Delalic's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which meetings -- be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Meetings of persons involved in the war presidency and the Konjic defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I told you clearly -- occasionally, on the upper floor, Mr. Delalic would come there. I did not see any persons meeting there, because I had no need to see them. If I went outside, I would not see anyone, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how many people worked in the communications centre -- just approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there when I was there, and two or three of my associates, experts and there were a couple of signals men in a shift, two or three -- anyway, they worked in shifts, they would rest for five or six hours and then continue, so there were quite a number of these signals men. Whether there were 10 or 12 or less, I did not count, because what was important to me was to know the status of the persons working with me, whether they were present or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Habiba Bukvic ever work in the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that there was Mira and another lady, Djina or something like that -- I am not quite sure about Habiba that you mentioned -- did you say Buklic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Bukvic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In addition to Mira, did Dina Pilas work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to Dina Pilas as Djina, I seem to remember the name Djina -- if that is the same person, I do not know -- later on, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How about Ismeta Pozder, did she ever work in the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this communications centre that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I know that girl very well, but I do not know that she worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. Sir, I know that you testified yesterday that you do not know exactly when Mr. Rizvanovic became your superior, but can you tell me approximately for how long Mr. Rizvanovic was your superior -- until what time approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until what time -- let me see. It would have been 18 or 19 April 1993 and then I moved to another position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, until April 1993; is that correct -- I am not sure that I heard correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you heard me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know exactly when Mr. Delalic became coordinator and for how long he served as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know when he became the coordinator and he was coordinator until he was appointed commander of TG1 in Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You testified you had seen Prosecution Exhibit 127, which is the document signed by Mr. Delalic and two other persons about the railroad. My question is: did you ever see any other documents signed by Mr. Delalic in his role as coordinator, or was that the only document that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that one document and I did not see any other documents. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when Mr. Delalic was coordinator, you indicated that he sometimes spent time in the field and, indeed, he was in the field when he was appointed commander of TG1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the role of coordinator for almost the entire time and I said that it started in 2 June and it went until about 26 July -- maybe it could have been only four or five days that we were not together and I told about the train thing and then the electric lines in those villages there, and then there was also the communications centre in his house, but he could not be there all the time; he had other things to look after -- supply of food and then everything that concerned the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is the answer to my question therefore "Yes", that he was sometimes in the field when he was coordinator and in fact he was in the field at the time he was appointed TG1 commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At the time when he was in the field, when he was appointed TG1 commander and you contacted him to tell him about his appointment, for approximately how long had Mr. Delalic been in the field during that time; in other words, without coming back to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was out in the field the entire month of June -- he may have come home occasionally to change clothes and it was his communications centre but it was also his home, so I could not monitor his comings and goings, but I know that he spent that entire month in the field. Maybe he occasionally came home for a couple of hours to change clothes or rest or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just make sure that there is not a miscommunication. Are you stating that Mr. Delalic was in the field for almost the entire month of June -- did I understand the month correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was in June with me and we worked on these problems that I described, but in July he was in Vranjske Stijene and that is what I stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think there may have been an interpretation problem. You stated you knew Mr. Mustafa Polutak. When he was commander of TG1, did he use the communications centre in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He used it occasionally, this communications centre in Konjic, but very frequently -- maybe once or twice when he needed to have some message sent to Sarajevo, because this communications centre in Pazaric was shelled quite frequently, so some of the equipment was damaged and then he used our own facility to send some messages over to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware that Mr. Polutak had an accident in early August, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not "Poletak"; it is "Polutak" and I was not aware of the accident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am sure that is not the last name I am going to mispronounce. It is very fair of you to try and correct that. When he was Tactical Group commander, what geographic zone was Mr. Polutak responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Polutak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really would not be able to tell you that. Strategy was not my job. My job was exclusively technical stuff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fair enough, Sir. After Mr. Delalic became commander of TG1, did he use the communications centre in his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes -- only sometimes though -- very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You have indicated that Sarajevo sometimes sent Mr. Delalic messages using this communications centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, if the equipment was damaged in Pazarici or there was no power, then they used our facility to communicate their messages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And if Sarajevo wanted to send a message by courier to Mr. Delalic, would they send that through the communications centre, or would they go directly to where Mr. Delalic was, the headquarters of TG1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how they thought about these things, how they would contemplate doing them, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When Mr. Delalic was -- were there problems in getting messages to Mr. Delalic from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes there were problems, sometimes not -- it all depended on the situation both in the city of Sarajevo, that is, the availability of gas and electricity and, also, it depended on us -- you never knew when you would get it or when you would not. Sometimes you would wait a day or even two days to send the message, because if the communications centres did not work, then you could not send these communications. In such cases, couriers were used then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there also problems in getting messages to the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. If it had to do with power shortages or with shelling, but if everything was okay, if the communications centre had regular supply of power, then that was not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that the order appointing Mr. Delalic head of the Tactical Group came by messenger from Fojnica and you contacted Mr. Delalic personally to tell him about it; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it happened so that, on that day -- I think it was in the afternoon, I was in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is fine -- if it is just "yes" you can say "yes" and I can go on to my next question. I wanted to ensure I understood you correctly before I went to my next question. When you contacted Mr. Delalic, did you contact him using the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, this communications centre, those outposts radio transmitters were out in the field, and they had a very different way of communicating. You used the FM communications and this is how we passed on the message to him, to Mr. Delalic, that he became one of the important persons in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was the order that you told Mr. Delalic about -- do you remember if the order was dated around this same time period, the end of July, or could the order have been dated in mid July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it should have been late July, because the courier who brought this order said that he travelled for two days, so if he had to travel for two days because of some misunderstanding with the HVO, then that could have been dated two days before he brought it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when this courier from Fojnica came, was this the first that you had heard about Mr. Delalic being appointed head of TG1, or had you received any kind of oral notification before that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the first time that I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you told Mr. Delalic about his appointment, did you read out the order, word for word, to him, or did you just interpret it for him and tell him the important parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not read it to him. The courier told us that he was going to replace Polutak. Since we knew who was Polutak, at least I knew who Polutak was, then I congratulated him on this, how shall I put it, promotion, so that I did not read the contents of this order -- I do not know if it was information on promotion or what. As I said, the courier told us that he was replacing Polutak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, Sir, did I understand you -- did you yourself even read the order from the courier? Even if you did not read it to Mr. Delalic, did you yourself read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, I did not. I did not read the order, because the courier told us that this is what happened, and I myself did not read the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, if I understand correctly, the courier came with an order -- the courier told you about the order. You immediately contacted Mr. Delalic and you never yourself looked at the order or told Mr. Delalic what was in the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the communications people did their job, and I just did it informally. I called him to congratulate him, and what kind of an order it was -- there was a text there, I know that there was a text.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, at some later point, did you ever see any other appointment order for Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Delalic gave orders to the TO or municipal headquarters, would he use the communications centre to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean as a commander of TG1?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that he was able to issue orders to the municipal staff. That is, I am not familiar with that, or to the municipal bodies. He was a separate body. He was his own unit and, as far as I could tell, these different TOs, these different staffs were supposed to send us a certain number of soldiers, but as I tell you, I am a technical person, so I do not know about these superiority things and chains of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. Am I correct that you stated that there were about 50 soldiers from Konjic who were assigned to TG1?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has stated several times that he did not know about these things and I think that it should not continue -- that these questions should not continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am asking him about something he explicitly stated in direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put it to him. If he does not know, he will say he does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand you yesterday to say there were about 50 soldiers from Konjic who were assigned to TG1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I do not know the exact number of soldiers. It is possible -- I said that it was possible that it was 50 soldiers, but whether it was more or less, I am not sure. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know from what unit or brigade these soldiers were, however many there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not Mr. Delalic was a superior to the staff of TG1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What type of a question is that? Are you asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was his own staff -- he was superior to that staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Mr. Delalic was superior to his own staff -- the staff of the TG1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he was appointed commander of this group, he certainly was superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood you correctly during your direct testimony, you would deny that you were ever a part of Mr. Delalic's staff when he was commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never, but, as I said, we worked on all technical projects, but, as to whether Mr. Delalic had any authority over me or these communications chiefs -- no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If Mr. Delalic reports that for a period of time when he was commander of Tactical Group 1 you were a member of his staff, he would be wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. The witness answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know what type of objection this is. What is the difficulty in him saying whether they are members of his Tactical Group or not? This question is not unfair. Please, answer the question whether you were part of Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never subordinate to Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question, Sir, directly was: so, if Mr. Delalic reported that you were a member of his staff when he was commander of TG1, he would be wrong; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Arsen Rizvanovic, your superior, was he ever commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Major Kevric was part of the command staff of TG1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- I do not believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How about Habiba Bukvic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- I have no idea. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Delalic was commander of Tactical Group 1 and he needed additional units, or he wanted a particular unit moved to a different location for battle, do you know how he would communicate his orders in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that method of work of the staff. I am a technical person and whatever I am told, I do. If I am told to set up a communications centre, that is what I do, but as far as the organisation and command, that is not what I did, and I was not concerned with that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, apart from setting up the communications centre, did you do anything other than that? Did you continue to operate it for Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked on the railroad until 7 January 1993 and parallel to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am limiting you to the communications centre -- apart from setting up the communications facilities, did you do anything with respect to communications, that is, organising how his future communications unit should be. Did you do anything other than setting up the facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did repairs of radio equipment, of these radio transmitters and I did that throughout this period. As I said yesterday, those two or three centres which we set up for the Oganj Operation, I also worked on that, so it was not just a single communications centre, so there were several communications centres which we set up as a technical team and, of course, doing some other telephone lines later on, but it is not part of the matter that we are discussing here right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. Sir, when you first began working with Mr. Delalic, and you stated you were with him frequently, were you present at a meeting with Mr. Delalic and a number of other persons when the problems in Celebici were discussed and Mr. Delalic suggested Mr. Mucic as commander of Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I made myself clear, I said at the very beginning that I saw Mr. Delalic for the first time when I actually met him -- that was on 2 June and that was the only working contact that I had with Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Mucic became commander of Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You stated, Sir, that sometimes Mr. Mucic would contact Mr. Delalic. Did I understand you correctly that you were not present during their conversations, so you do not know the subject matter of their conversations?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection. I did not hear this witness saying ever that Mr. Mucic contacted Mr. Delalic, so I think the question is not in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought he did, but, if not, let me ask the question. Did you state during your testimony yesterday that, on occasion, Mr. Mucic would contact Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that we were called up to set in operation a telephone exchange in the Celebici barracks in August. As for Pavo, that he contacted somebody and talked to somebody, and especially Zejnil, I did not see that. You have the minutes, you have the transcript and you can check. I do not remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who asked you to fix the telephones in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The head of the communications, upon approval of the commander of the TO -- probably somebody from the barracks had asked for it, because if there was a failure, they must have asked for it to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you went out to the Celebici barracks after being called there by Pavo Mucic, the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am saying again, it is possible that Pavo made the call, but I did go to the Celebici barracks to repair the telephones which were not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you went to Celebici, who went with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went and there was Mr. Dulic, a telecommunications engineer, who was familiar with Iskra's telephone exchanges -- he had a better knowledge of them than I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Rizvanovic go with you to fix the phones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember -- possibly he may have driven us there and come back to fetch us, but I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what part of the camp did you go into? In particular, what buildings did you go into? Are you familiar with the building that is referred to as the reception building and the building that is referred to as the command building? If you are not, Sir, there is a model in front of you and maybe, if you are not familiar with those terms, maybe you can just point to us and show us the building or buildings that you went to when you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to this building here to the left (witness indicates with pointer). This part here is probably the reception and this office where the telephone exchange was, I think it is this window in the middle -- left from the entrance -- I assume that was the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say, Sir, then that you did not go into the reception building at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no need to go to the reception building. There was a guard there. I did not communicate with him. We passed on directly and looked for the telephone exchange. Of course, a soldier met us there and asked what we wanted. We said that we had come to repair the telephone exchange. He said, "Please, go ahead" and we went to the office in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Mucic when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see -- I did not personally know Mr. Mucic at the time. I may have seen him, because if he was there, he should have contacted with us. If Mr. Rizvanovic had brought us there, then he should have contacted him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Was anybody so introduced to you -- as Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was a woman and she said, "The warden is in the next office and that is where the telephone exchange is, too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly answer the question of counsel, whether you saw Mr. Mucic there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you went into the next office where the telephone exchange was, was the warden there?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said the warden was in the next room and the follow-up question was whether he saw the warden in the next room. So what is the objection about?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Allow me to explain, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is nothing to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: He said he did not know Mucic at the time, that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Then he was told the warden was in the next room -- that is what he was told. If he then went and saw the warden, then that is what the counsel is trying to find out, whether he went to see the warden in the next room. It is quite a legitimate and proper question to ask. Whether he knew him or not, he would have seen who was the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The warden, yes, but not Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are wasting the time of counsel. Please, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you went into the next office where the telephone exchange was, was the warden present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that he was present, because this lady told me, "In the next office is the warden's office and that is where the telephone exchange is which is faulty."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you state yesterday that, from the time the train began working in early June, the families of the detained persons were allowed to visit the prisoners in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Were allowed to use the train -- the first time they were allowed to use the train.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Presumably they would be using the train. My question, Sir, is: is it correct that you stated that the families of the detainees were allowed to use the train and beginning in early June they used the train to visit their family members detained in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, everyone had transportation free of charge. You could see that on the tape -- if there was a tape, I was a participant in the filming, there were several cameras used and the person in charge of the organisation of transportation, Mr. Buntic, said that a timetable had been made and according to that timetable for the trains, all persons who needed to travel could use the train free of charge on the line from Pazarici to Jablanica, so everyone could use the train -- whoever needed to use it could use it, free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Relax a little bit. I think you are on the right part when you said the train was free to everyone and it was legitimate to understand that -- everybody, how everybody, whether or not they were families of detainees, would use the train, free of charge. Nobody was stopped from using the train, so you could have answered the question without all this apprehension you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone could use the train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what you have said. They could be families of detainees or anyone else, anyone could use it. That is what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my specific question is not whether or not anyone had to pay . Is it your testimony that families of detainees were allowed to visit prisoners in Celebici from the beginning of June when the train started running?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was not a warden there. He said the train could be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would agree with that. That is not what he testified to yesterday. Yesterday he was more explicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Read that portion to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not have it right in front of me, which is why I am trying to clarify -- which is why my question was, "Did I understand you correctly?" Sir, do you know when the detainees' families were allowed to visit prisoners in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact, your own witness -- the doctor's wife said that she used that train to go to Celebici -- I do not want to mention the doctor's name, because that is a protected witness -- but she said she used that train to go to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: On the return, she could not and she walked back, but she used the train for going to the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. My question has to do with the timing and whether or not this witness knows whether or not, beginning in early June, people were allowed to visit their family members in Celebici. If he knows, he can say so. If he does not know, obviously he can say, "I do not know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He can speak about the use of the train.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He cannot speak about whether or not they were allowed to visit the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would agree with that. Is it correct that you have no idea whether or not the families of detained persons were allowed actually to visit the detainees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I do not even know why you ask him such a question. Does he really need to go into that, whether they were visiting their families? We have had evidence here that members of their families visited them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am asking it, because he stated it in direct testimony and I think timing of when visits may or may not have been allowed is relevant. That is why I am asking the question. Is it correct you do not know whether or not families were allowed to visit detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was permitted -- visits of family members were permitted and that they used the train for that purpose. Some people did; others did not, that did not need to be transported by train.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How exactly do you know that visits were permitted and from what time period were they permitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably from the day they were detained. A part of my acquaintances were detained and their wives addressed me at the railway station and asked me when visits were allowed and I said that visits were allowed every day and I knew that others were using the train -- 6 or 7 June, until then I did not know that there was a prison there at all, until 7 June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me move on, Sir. Sir, you testified in direct about some communication with the supreme command, about the visit of the Red Cross to Celebici camp. You were aware that ultimately Mr. Delalic was the person who was supposed to arrange this visit; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of the fact that Mr. Delalic was to arrange that visit. In my statement that I made some time in 1996, I did not pay much attention to the sequence of events. I said that this had happened and that Zejnil called, but, as far as I remember, in the next sentence I already corrected myself and said that Mr. Delalic had called us up in the communications centre, saying that this should be allowed, because they had some problems with their car and that we should see what was the hitch with the TO staff regarding allowing their visit and then we contacted the TO staff and they replied immediately that the visit of the International Red Cross should be organised to the prison or the prisons -- the prison in Celebici. I do not know which one. Anyway, all it said was that the visit of the Red Cross should be organised. After that, I do not remember exactly whether it was that day or the next day, a short telegram arrived and this was forwarded on to Sarajevo. Whether the answer came back to Zejnil Delalic or not, I have no idea. I know that it was forwarded on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is your prior statement incorrect when you stated that the Red Cross gave their report to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say it was incorrect, but when this lady, the investigator, authorised by the Defence to take my statement -- she probably turned around the word order so that the meaning of the sentence was changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you said you are aware that the report was sent through the communications centre to Sarajevo. I assume then, Sir, that you are aware that the report was extremely critical of the conditions in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I said a short report had been sent in the direction of Sarajevo, but, if necessary, I will repeat 100 times: I did not read all those documents; I did not need to do that. I am a technical person. Sometimes I would hand a document to somebody and tell him that it was an urgent thing that had to be sent if the others were busy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I understand, Sir, you have no idea that it was in the Red Cross report -- is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea, because I did not read the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is fair enough, Sir. You mentioned this prior statement you gave. Would you agree with me, and can you tell me if this is a mistake or not, that in your prior statement you stated that you went to Celebici after being called there by Pavo Mucic, the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, because, according to that statement of mine, because I assumed he was the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would also agree with me, would you not, that you do not know who Mr. Mucic's superior was with respect to Celebici camp, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea who was superior to any gentlemen in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he make a statement to an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He made a statement to a representative from the Defence, not to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, although she introduced herself to you here in court, am I correct that you had met Ms. McMurrey before yesterday -- the blonde woman who represents Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yesterday in court was the first time you ever met her, or anyone who represents the Landzo Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw her around. I did not know who she was -- I saw her walking around but I did not know who she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Had you ever talked with anyone working as part of the Landzo Defence about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to my testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know Mr. Rajko Gotovac and a Marijan Rajic, persons who were foresters in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Rajko Gotovac and Marijan Rajic -- persons who were foresters in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know Gotovac, and this other one could be Marijan Rajic, this other one. Maybe it is a printing error.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was that person a forester?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan was a forester and he lived near a road tunnel in Celebici on the left side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that at some time Mr. Rajic and another person had an accident in a chalk mine which caused some burns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Babic, Mirko, had an accident with this chalk pit near his village of Bjelovcina that where he resided.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to ask you about that in a minute. I am asking you now whether you know that Mr. Rajic is a person in fact who had an accident in a chalk mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, because he was working with Mr. Babic in the chalk mine. I did not see Marijan in that situation but I did see Babic in that situation and I was saying how I saw Babic at the railway station waiting for the train.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Babic, was he wearing shorts rather than long pants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was bandaged -- his legs were bandaged. What kind of trousers he was wearing, I really do not know whether they were long or short.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were the bandages under his trousers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bandages were below his knee.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there trousers covering the bandages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether his trousers were rolled up, or whether he was wearing shorts, I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was anyone else with you on this occasion, or with Mr. Babic when you saw the bandages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think his late brother, Branko, was with him, because at the time he was working at the railroads. I think he was with me when he came by -- I assume so, but I am not sure of that, because I remember this about Mirko, how he had got burnt working on the chalk mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So other than his late brother, you are not aware of anyone else who was present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were both legs bandaged, or just one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember whether or not the bandages went all the way from the knee to the ankle, or was it just part of the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the ankle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The interpreters did not necessarily hear you. Can you just repeat your answer, Sir? What part of his leg was bandaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Below the knee towards the ankle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: After his leg was not bandaged, you never had the occasion to see Mr. Babic's leg again, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, because he did not come to the railway station every day, and that was where I worked, so I saw him there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you were shown a picture and you recognised it as Mr. Babic's leg and you further testified about the cause of the injury on Mr. Babic's leg. Sir, my question is: can you normally recognise a person merely by looking at a picture of their shin?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. The question that I asked him was whether that was the location of the burn on Mr. Babic's leg, not whether he recognised the leg of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That was the leg of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Whether that was the location of the injury that he had seen before, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel is entitled to ask whether you can recognise a person from the area where there was an injury -- whether, by looking at the shin, you identify that as that of the other person. If he cannot, he should say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: are you in a position to recognise persons just by looking at photographs of their shin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise the person from his portrait, not from his leg -- I was first shown a photograph of his head and shoulders, and normally, after that, if somebody asks him whether his leg was burnt and whether this was a leg or an arm, and it was obvious that this was a leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you stated that the injury shown on the photograph was the result of the burn he got from the lime, I am correct, Sir, that you yourself do not know where he got that injury and in fact you yourself do not know whether or not Mr. Landzo set Mr. Babic on fire when he was detained in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are adding something different. He did not extend it to any other thing. He indicated the type of injury which he thought Mr. Babic had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe I will just ask him to clarify. When you stated yesterday, Sir, in your examination, when shown the photograph, "That is the injury due to the burn that he got from the lime" -- that is not actually correct, is it -- you do not actually know where that injury is from, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the fact that, as I said a moment ago, I saw the man with bandages on his leg, so I assumed that that could be that burn, because it is familiar knowledge that the man was burnt in the lime several years before the war. I do not know exactly how many, so that is why I believe that that was the burn. I am not claiming now that this was that particular burn, but what I do know is that he did suffer a burn on his legs and it is possible that this could be that burn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember the FM radio frequency on which Konjic could be reached and whether or not it was 3704.3 MHz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, 370 -- what did you say -- 370 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That frequency is not an ultra short-wave frequency -- this is a short-wave frequency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, I think we will have to break until 12 and we will continue at noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I will have either no or one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have not understood correctly, or I may have misstated my answer, but when asked by the Defence attorney, that is, Ms. McMurrey, the Defence counsel of Mr. Landzo, that I did not see her before I came here to The Hague, to this Tribunal -- now, that is true, but, if the question concerned whether I saw her in the Tribunal, then the answer would be yes, we were in touch before I entered the courtroom. We had a short conversation with the entire team, and they asked me several questions -- each one of them. At that time I did not know who represented whom in this case, with the exception of Ms. Residovic, and I would like you to accept this answer as truthful and correct and would appreciate that. I also apologise to Madam Prosecutor, and I would like her to accept this answer, because, when you first asked me, I did not understand it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sultanic. What we advise you to do -- calm down and do not be too apprehensive, and answer questions in the way you get them and you will be alright. Do not anticipate too much. The questions normally follow from your own answers and then, if you are relaxed, you will have no problems at all. Thank you very much. You may continue, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only one question, your Honours. Sir, do you know what location is 3704.3 MHz in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The location 3704.3, it does not exist. It is a frequency of one of the radio stations and that could change on a daily basis, or maybe a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just one question. Which leg of Mr. Babic did you see bandaged -- right or left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could not tell. I was not paying attention to those details at the time, because I kind of just took it as a joke, because, you know, he would like to drink a little bit and maybe it was in poor taste -- he was burned so much, but I was not paying any attention to which leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have only two questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, you said that many people were wearing uniforms and that for a while there was no difference between the civilians and soldiers. Could you tell me now, when carrying out your duties and activities, were there any differences between the duties carried out by soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I pointed out that it was kind of a fashion to wear uniforms, but, as far as the duties, the jobs, are concerned, the difference was absolute. The soldiers were mobilised and had to do whatever they had to do and the civilians worked for different civilian enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated to the Prosecutor that you did not know Habiba Bukvic but did you know a certain Mira and Djina, can you tell me now whether Mira and Djina worked in the communication centre of the TO staff which was located in the house of Mr. Delalic and on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not work at the communications centre, because it was a hard job -- they only worked in the house -- I think that they just worked in Zejnil Delalic's residence, so I saw them there, but they would not enter the communications centre. As a rule, the communications centre has to have certain restricted access, so no, persons who do not work there should not have access to it, so they did not work there, and none of these women, some of whom were married and some who were not, were not entering there. They just went about certain jobs which was part of the housework in Zejnil Delalic's residence on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, just one additional question, please. Did Zejnil Delalic have anything to do with issuing orders to have the communications centre set up in his residence -- in his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He should not have had anything to do with that, because I think it was the TO staff that was supposed to set it up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one clarification, with your permission. Mr. Sultanic, can we say that in the latter part of August 1992 you did not know Mr. Zdravko Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is the end of this witness's testimony. Thank you very much, Mr. Sultanic. We are very grateful for your assistance and your ability to assist here. You can now be discharged. Will you now call your next witness? You are now discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please call the next Defence witness. The next witness is Sefkija Kevric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down, take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. SEFKIJA KEVRIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir. Will you please introduce yourself -- could you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Sefkija Kevric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, before I proceed with my questions, let me give you a very short technical explanation. My questions and your answers need to be interpreted in order for our conversation to be understandable to everybody in the courtroom and for it to be taken down on the record. So, please, when you hear a question, listen to its interpretation coming through the headphones on the desk and, only when you hear that it is completed, answer my question. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Kevric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Dragan Selo in the Jablanica municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina on 22 April 1953.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background and what is your citizenship, Sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak and a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is your education and where you received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from high school in 1983, the Military Economic Academy in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by profession, Mr. Kevric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an officer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, you are a professional soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a professional soldier of the former Yugoslav People's Army and now I am an officer -- a commissioned officer of the Bosnian Federation Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, where were you in early April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early April 1992 I was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From where did you come to Banja Luka on the very eve of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a commissioned officer of the former JNA, I was stationed in Ljubljana in the Republic of Slovenia and when the conflict broke out in Slovenia, with the 14th Corps, on 12 June 1992, we were transferred to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, could you be wrong about the -- would you be wrong about the year of your transfer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies, it was in 1991, not 1992 .

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time in the spring of 1992 when you came to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my service in Banja Luka I realised that the Yugoslav People's Army was no longer the people's army -- that is, it did not belong to all people, that it was just the Serb people's army, which was protecting just one people, and in the morning hours of 13 April 1992 I fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your specialisation as a commissioned officer of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commissioned officer of the former JNA -- my specialisation was logistics, that is, quartermaster.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your rank in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former JNA, I had the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your rank in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina army I have a rank of a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When on 13 April 1992 you arrived in Konjic, did you report to certain structures there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon arrival in Konjic on 13 April 1992 I reported to the municipal TO staff in Konjic. I did not start working right away -- I only started working on 17 April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reported to the municipal staff of the TO Konjic, could you tell us who was the commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I reported, the commander of the TO staff was Mr. Smajo Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you started working on the 17th, that is, at the municipal staff of the TO Konjic, what post did you start working at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I started working, I worked as a logistics officer -- I was appointed the assistant commander for logistics by the new commander, Enver Redzepovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did the commander of the municipal staff of the TO Konjic change, that is, when Mr. Prevljak left and Mr. Redzepovic assumed that post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic started working on the 17th as commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what were the competencies of the municipal assembly with regard to the appointment of the commander -- who confirmed such appointments in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period and according to the law which was in force in the former Yugoslavia, there was the presidency and it was the body which confirmed this. However, later, the presidency ceased having this role.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, did I understand you correctly? You are referring to the presidency of the republic, or the SFRY -- I did not understand you well. To whom was the TO headquarters subordinate -- that is what you started explaining -- before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a republican staff, then there were district staffs and municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in Konjic, Mr. Kevric, in this TO staff where you started working as a logistics officer, was Mr. Zejnil Delalic a member of this staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic was not a member of the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, at the time when you arrived in Konjic, which was on the 13th and then you started working on the 17th, in that period did Mr. Delalic have any military post in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic had no military post in the municipality, that is, in the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before your coming to Konjic in April 1992, did you know Mr. Delalic at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never met Mr. Zejnil Delalic prior to April 1992. I knew his three brothers, but not him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, did you meet Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him in the town of Konjic on 18 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you met him, what was he doing -- what kind of activities was he engaged in when you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic was a civilian and talking to him, he offered to assist me in supplying and equipping the municipal staff of Konjic. He told me that he had business contacts, that he knew a large number of people, and that he could help me with supplies and all the equipment, technical equipment and communications equipment that we needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The things you discussed with Mr. Delalic, that is, the possibility of obtaining supplies, was this for you, as a man responsible for logistics in the TO, of significance at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very important indeed, because the TO staff of Konjic at the time did not have any technical or material resources or communications equipment or quartermaster supplies -- it did not have food depots, because all the warehouses were located in the Ljuta barracks, which the Yugoslav People's Army was guarding.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you have any arms for TO members who had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, we had certain quantities of weapons, mostly hunting weapons -- weapons legally held and for which individuals had licences to wear those weapons. The MUP also had some weapons and persons who sought to purchase weapons with their own funds, because of the danger of war -- we had no other sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, did you, in April 1992, take over a certain quantity of weapons from one of the barracks of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second decade of the month of April some weapons were taken over from the Celebici barracks and some other technical and material resources, but small quantities -- a unit of MUP and a small number of TO members took over the Celebici barracks peacefully. They took over the weapons and they transferred them to the farm at Ovcari. According to lists, a part of those weapons were issued to members of the units that participated in the take-over of the Celebici barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, are you aware whether any assignment with respect to the take-over of the Celebici barracks was given to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic had the task of taking over those weapons and transferring them in a motor vehicle to Ovcari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take over those weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally took over weapons, together with Sadih Dzumka, known as Diksa, and I stored it in the warehouse at the farm at Ovcari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For how long were you a member of the TO staff, or later the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member from 17 April 1992 until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have just asked you about some activities in the month of April. In view of the fact that you were a member of the TO staff, do you know what was happening in the first half of May 1992, in terms of military activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first half of May 1992, we captured the Ljuta barracks, we took over a certain part of the armament -- we did not manage to take everything, because the Yugoslav People's Army air force hit the depot of the 114th Brigade, so that it was destroyed. We took over the facility D0, known as "Ark", which is the reserve command post of the army, the underground facility there, and we captured the facility Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After this, Mr. Kevric, did all members of the Yugoslav People's Army who did not join the ranks of Territorial Defence -- did they all abandon Konjic? Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the Yugoslav People's Army, through a side exit of the facility D0, abandoned the facility and, together with the members who were stationed at Zlatar, they were transferred by helicopter, except for warrant officer Serif Grabovica, whom they did not wish to take in the helicopter, even though he was working with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, do you know what were the activities of Mr. Delalic in that period? We are talking about the first two decades of the month of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, at the beginning of April -- at the beginning of -- I am sorry, at the beginning of May, was authorised to go to Zagreb to obtain certain quantities of material -- technical resources, communication equipment and quartermaster supplies. I may not be quite precise about this, but he stayed in Zagreb until 19 or 20 May and, before Mr. Zejnil Delalic returned, a convoy reached Celebici with weapons and material technical supplies. A day or two later, Mr. Delalic arrived with another two or three truck loads of materiel and quartermaster supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us, Mr. Kevric, that, for the whole of 1992, you were a member of the Territorial Defence staff from 17 April. Then you can certainly tell the court whether that Territorial Defence staff was a small staff, a medium sized one, or one compared to a more developed entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff we had at the time was a large staff that corresponded to a developed structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some time in April did the Territorial Defence staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina require from your staff certain information about persons who may be engaged in the staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.
